drills.q: What is the default value of -XX:MaxGCPauseMillis, and is it a guarantee?
drills.a: 200ms, and it's a soft target G1 tries to hit by sizing young-gen and mixed-GC work -- not a hard guarantee.

drills.q: What size threshold makes an object 'humongous' in G1?
drills.a: Larger than 50% of the region size.

drills.q: Since which JDK version has G1 been the default collector?
A team doubles -Xmx to 'fix' GC pauses and pauses get worse, not better. Explain why.
drills.a: A bigger heap means more live data to scan and compact during a collection, which can lengthen individual pause duration even while reducing how often collections happen. Whether more heap helps depends on whether the problem is frequency-driven or scan-cost-driven -- check the GC log before resizing.

drills.q: Explain the mechanism that lets ZGC relocate objects concurrently without stopping the application to fix up references.
drills.a: Colored pointers encode object state (marked, remapped) in unused high bits of the 64-bit pointer. Every reference read goes through a load barrier that checks those bits and transparently redirects/fixes a stale reference on the spot if the object moved -- references self-heal lazily on next access instead of requiring a stop-the-world fixup pass.

drills.q: A service switches from G1 to ZGC for a nightly batch ETL job with no latency SLO, and total job time gets worse. Diagnose.
drills.a: ZGC's structural 15-30% memory / 5-10% CPU overhead (the cost of concurrent relocation) was paid for a throughput-bound workload with no pause-time requirement to benefit from -- the switch should be reverted to G1, since ZGC's value proposition (low pause time) was never relevant here.

drills.q: What specific failure mode ended CMS's use in production, and name its G1 analog.
drills.a: CMS never compacted concurrently, so old-gen fragmentation eventually left no contiguous space for a large allocation, forcing a full single-threaded stop-the-world compaction ('concurrent mode failure'). G1's analog is falling back to a Full GC when allocation outpaces concurrent marking -- same underlying class of failure: a concurrent collector that falls behind degrades to a stop-the-world pause.

drills.q: A hot method is repeatedly compiled, discarded, and recompiled according to JFR's jdk.Deoptimization events. What's the likely root cause and the code-level fix?
drills.a: C2 compiled the method assuming a call site was monomorphic (based on C1's profiling data); a second concrete implementation later showed up, invalidating the specialized inlined code, forcing deoptimization back to the interpreter and eventual recompilation with corrected polymorphic data -- if this repeats, the call site is thrashing. Fix: reduce polymorphism at that call site if possible (bound an unbounded strategy/plugin pattern, avoid heavy reflection-based dispatch there).

drills.q: Design the diagnostic sequence for 'the service is slow' before touching any JVM flag.
drills.a: Capture a GC log (-Xlog:gc*) and a JFR recording (or attach one live) first. Read the GC log triage: frequent short young GCs are usually fine; climbing frequency and pause length together signals working-set growth; Pause Full (Allocation Failure) signals the G1 fallback failure mode; a shrinking before->after reclaim gap over time signals a leak. Only after the log/JFR evidence points to a specific mechanism (heap sizing, humongous objects, JIT deopt, an actual leak) do you touch a flag -- guessing at flags without log evidence risks subtle regressions.

drills.q: Explain why Generational ZGC displaced non-generational ZGC entirely (JEP 490) rather than the two modes coexisting.
drills.a: Non-generational ZGC treated every object uniformly with no cheap young-gen fast path, costing real throughput on allocation-heavy workloads since short-lived objects paid the same barrier/relocation overhead as long-lived ones. Generational ZGC (default since JDK 23, JEP 474) cut CPU overhead roughly 30-40% for allocation-heavy workloads and won essentially every benchmark, so non-generational mode was removed to reduce long-term maintenance burden for a mode nobody had a reason to prefer.

drills.q: A JMH-less benchmark shows a code change is 3x faster locally, but production load tests show no measurable difference. What's the most likely explanation?
drills.a: The local benchmark measured JIT warm-up cost (interpreter and C1 tiers) rather than steady-state C2-optimized throughput, since it had no explicit warm-up phase discarded before measurement. Rerun with JMH's @Warmup iterations, or discard the first several seconds/minutes of a load test before computing throughput/latency.
